answer: With nuts_sampler='nutpie', PyMC hands sampling off to the nutpie library, which runs its own Rust sampling loop and progress reporting - it does not go through PyMC's ProgressBarManager, so your monkeypatch of ProgressBarManager.update is simply never called for that backend. Two fixes: (1) drop nuts_sampler='nutpie' and use PyMC's default NUTS sampler, which does call ProgressBarManager/callback; or (2) keep nutpie but pass its own progress/callback options (nutpie.sample accepts a progress_type or callback argument) instead of patching PyMC's class. Also beware multiprocessing: if chains>1 and cores>1, each chain samples in a separate process, so a callback patched in the main process won't fire there either - set cores=1 (or chains=1) so sampling stays in-process and your Streamlit st.progress calls, made from the same thread that's blocking on pm.sample, actually execute. For the default sampler, prefer PyMC's built-in callback= argument of pm.sample() over monkeypatching internals, since that's the supported hook for per-draw progress.

.map()/.apply() returns a single Series whose elements happen to be tuples; assigning it to three columns at once doesn't auto-unpack the way you want, and Python's `a, b, c = series` tries to unpack the Series itself, not each element. Convert the tuple results into their own DataFrame instead:
mydf[['d3','d2','d1']] = mydf['mynum'].apply(lambda x: last_3_divisions(x, 2), result_type='expand')
or, keeping map():
results = mydf['mynum'].map(lambda x: last_3_divisions(x, 2))
mydf[['d3','d2','d1']] = pd.DataFrame(results.tolist(), index=mydf.index)
Either pattern turns the Series-of-tuples into a proper 2D structure with matching column count, which pandas can then assign column-by-column. Note result_type is an apply-only keyword, not available on .map().

The installed PyQt5-stubs package ships only the single-argument connect overload, so any 2-arg call (adding a Qt.ConnectionType) fails mypy regardless of what your code does at runtime. Pragmatically, just scope a targeted ignore:
btn.clicked.connect(clicked, QtCore.Qt.QueuedConnection)  # type: ignore[call-arg]
If you want a real fix via custom stubs, your override must actually be discovered: add the stubs/ folder's path to mypy_path in mypy.ini/pyproject.toml (or the MYPYPATH env var) - a stubs/ directory sitting next to your code isn't picked up automatically. Also, when overriding a class from an installed stub package, you must redeclare every overload you want (including the original 1-arg one), not just append the new 2-arg overload, or you silently lose the other signatures. A cleaner long-term option is wrapping connections through a small typed helper function that has the type: ignore in exactly one place, so call sites stay clean.

A NameError for np at call time (not an ImportError at import time) means Model.py's `import numpy as np` line isn't actually executing in the version currently loaded into memory - a failed module import would raise ImportError/ModuleNotFoundError, not a later NameError. The classic Jupyter cause: once a module is imported it's cached in sys.modules, and editing the .py file afterward does NOT re-run its top-level code unless you restart the kernel or use autoreload. If Model.py originally lacked or had a broken numpy import and you fixed it later, the running kernel still holds the stale version. Fix: restart the kernel, or add at the very top of the notebook, before your imports:
%load_ext autoreload
%autoreload 2
Also check for a stale __pycache__ under library/, and make sure there isn't a second Model.py earlier on sys.path shadowing the real one.

On Windows, the console window is the process's controlling terminal - closing it sends a close signal that kills everything attached, which is why the red X is dangerous. The standard fix is to stop relying on that console entirely: launch with pythonw.exe (no console at all) and build your own in-app log viewer instead of watching a terminal. Add a QPlainTextEdit (in a dock widget or separate non-modal window) fed via a logging.Handler subclass whose emit() pushes text through a Qt signal (queued connection) to append safely from any thread - real-time output with no closable terminal. Since you already duplicate output to a log file, a lower-effort alternative is to run headless (pythonw, output only to file) and tail that file from an independent window that isn't the app's own console, e.g. `Get-Content -Wait app.log` in a separate PowerShell window - closing that window doesn't touch the app's process.

_msi (and the msilib package wrapping it) is a Windows-only CPython extension module built into the standard library - it isn't a PyPI package, so pip install python-msi / pymsilib can't provide it; those installs are no-ops here. Two likely causes: (1) your venv's base Python install is missing/corrupted DLLs/_msi.pyd - repair-install that exact Python version from python.org (Modify/Repair) so the file exists under <PythonInstall>\DLLs, then recreate the venv; or (2), more likely if the rebuild picked up a newer interpreter: msilib/_msi was deprecated and then removed from the standard library in Python 3.13. If your corrupted venv was on an older Python and the fresh rebuild grabbed 3.13, no repair brings it back - recreate the venv with Python 3.12 or earlier, or find/patch whatever dependency imports msilib (often pulled in indirectly by setuptools/distutils-adjacent tooling) to avoid that import on 3.13.

This happens because every group in your core pattern is optional (M{0,4}, D?C{0,3}, etc.), so the engine can satisfy the lookahead and \b anchors while consuming zero characters - a legal but useless empty match. There's no simple quantifier tweak that forbids 'all groups empty' without restructuring the alternation, so the standard, robust fix is to filter empty matches after the fact rather than fighting the regex:
matches = [m.group() for m in re.finditer(pattern, text, re.IGNORECASE) if m.group()]
This is the normal, accepted way to handle patterns that can validly match a zero-width position (re.finditer will happily return them). Building the constraint into the pattern itself would require the alternation to consume at least one character via an atomic/possessive construct, which Python's re module doesn't support cleanly - which is exactly why a post-filter (or the third-party regex module) is the pragmatic answer here rather than a purely regex-only fix.

It can serialize/deserialize correctly, but only if every custom layer involved - not just UPDoubleConv - is properly registered and implements a complete get_config/from_config; your snippet doesn't show DoubleConv's, and it must include everything its __init__ needs (e.g. spatial_dim). Nesting a custom layer inside a plain tf.keras.Sequential is fine in modern Keras as long as: each custom layer is decorated with @register_keras_serializable, get_config() returns everything needed to reconstruct it (including inherited kwargs via super().get_config()), and you save with the native Keras v3 format (model.save('model.keras')) rather than legacy HDF5, since v3 handles nested Sequential/custom objects far more reliably. Don't just assume it works - verify directly: config = model.get_config(); rebuilt = tf.keras.Model.from_config(config), or save to a temp .keras file, reload, and compare predictions on a fixed input before/after. That round-trip test is the only reliable way to confirm full serializability here.

This is CPython's own contextlib._GeneratorContextManager.__exit__ doing `exc.__traceback__ = traceback` to keep the traceback clean when a generator-based context manager re-raises the same exception object unchanged after gen.throw() - that's normal, longstanding stdlib behavior, not a bug in your code. It fails because minio.error.S3Error is (as of a recent minio-py release) implemented as a frozen dataclass exception. A frozen dataclass overrides __setattr__ to reject any attribute assignment, including inherited BaseException attributes like __traceback__ - so the moment stdlib exception-propagation machinery tries to mutate it, you get FrozenInstanceError instead of the real S3Error. This is effectively a bug/incompatibility in minio-py: exception classes generally shouldn't be frozen dataclasses. Fixes: pin/downgrade minio to a version where S3Error isn't frozen, check whether a newer release already fixed it, or file an upstream issue. Avoiding contextlib.contextmanager around that call may sidestep it but doesn't address the root cause.

The _pb2.py file is intentionally hard to statically analyze since classes are built dynamically via descriptor builder calls. The standard fix is to have protoc also generate a .pyi stub alongside the .py:
protoc -I=. --python_out=. --pyi_out=. person.proto
This produces person_pb2.pyi with a proper `class Person(Message): name: str; address: str; age: int ...` declaration. Pylance/pyright read .pyi files directly and will resolve `from person_pb2 import Person` correctly, with full attribute/type checking, without touching the generated .py. The --pyi_out flag has long been supported by protoc and is the officially recommended way to get IDE support. For richer stubs (more precise typing, oneof helpers), use the mypy-protobuf plugin instead: protoc --python_out=. --mypy_out=. person.proto, which produces more detailed .pyi than protoc's built-in generator. Regenerate the .pyi whenever the .proto changes and commit it alongside the generated .py.

Yes, in the normal case: pip identifies packages by their normalized distribution/project name (per PEP 503 - case-insensitive, with -, _, and . all treated as equivalent), so pip install Some-Package and pip uninstall some_package refer to the same thing, which is why your version/extras/dependency exceptions don't affect it. The one case beyond what you excluded: if you install from a local path, a wheel/sdist file, or a VCS URL (pip install ./mydir, pip install ./mypkg-1.0-py3-none-any.whl, pip install git+https://...), the string you typed to install is not necessarily the name to uninstall - pip still uninstalls by the package's declared distribution name from its metadata (the name field in pyproject.toml/setup.py), which can differ from the folder/file/URL name. So for a normal `pip install <name-from-pypi>`, uninstall with the same name; for local/VCS installs, check `pip show <guessed-name>` or `pip list` first to find the actual registered name.

There's no exact one-word equivalent, but Start-Process gets you there because, unlike just running `python my_program.py` in the console (which becomes a child tied to that console), Start-Process launches a genuinely separate process not attached to the terminal's console:
Start-Process -FilePath python -ArgumentList "my_program.py" -WindowStyle Hidden -RedirectStandardOutput out.log -RedirectStandardError err.log
Closing the PowerShell window afterward won't kill it. (-WindowStyle Hidden and -NoNewWindow are mutually exclusive - use Hidden since you want no visible window.) For the 'subprocesses should also survive' requirement, make sure your Python code spawns children via subprocess with creationflags=subprocess.CREATE_NEW_PROCESS_GROUP (or DETACHED_PROCESS) on Windows, otherwise grandchildren can still be tied to the console's process group and die with it. If you need survival across user logoff too, Start-Process isn't enough - use Task Scheduler (schtasks) with 'run whether user is logged on or not,' or run it as a service via nssm.

These are two different things. The docs' 'uv will not build it by default' statement is about implicit packaging during uv run/uv sync - i.e., uv won't try to install your own project into its environment as an editable/built package unless it looks like a real installable project (has [build-system], or uv infers tool.uv.package). It is not a statement about the `uv build` command. When you explicitly run `uv build`, you're directly requesting a build, so uv falls back to a default backend (here, classic setuptools - that's why you see 'running egg_info'/'running sdist', standard setuptools output) to produce something, even without an explicit [build-system] table. This is expected: `uv build` always tries to build regardless of [build-system] presence; the 'won't build by default' guarantee applies only to uv's automatic/implicit packaging during commands like `uv run`/`uv sync`. If you don't want `uv init`-created projects to be buildable at all, add `package = false` under `[tool.uv]`.

This is almost always multiple Python interpreters on the machine disagreeing with each other: the Software Manager/apt install of pandas goes into the system Python's site-packages, but whatever interpreter your IDE or `python`/`python3` command actually runs may be a different one (a venv, a different python3.x, a Store/Snap python, etc.) that doesn't see those packages. Confirm exactly which interpreter is failing:
python3 -c "import sys; print(sys.executable)"
then install pandas explicitly into that same interpreter:
/that/exact/path/python3 -m pip install pandas
If you're using a venv, note venvs are isolated by default - packages installed via the OS package manager or a plain global pip never appear inside an activated venv unless it was created with --system-site-packages. Also check your IDE's configured interpreter/kernel matches the one you tested in the terminal, since IDEs often silently default to a different Python than expected after switching OSes.

This is expected behavior of HF datasets, not a bug in your function - Arrow-backed dataset columns must be homogeneous in schema, so when .map() builds the 'content' column (a list of structs), it unions the keys seen across all your dicts ({'type','text'} from the text-only entries and {'type','text','image'} from the image entry) into one struct schema, and back-fills any dict missing a key with null - hence 'image': None appearing even in your text-only system message. It's not something create_conversation does wrong; you can't easily keep per-row heterogeneous dict shapes in a mapped Arrow dataset. In practice this is harmless - chat-template/collation code typically only looks at 'type' and ignores irrelevant keys. If it truly causes downstream problems, strip the null image keys after mapping with a second .map() pass that filters None-valued entries out of each content dict, rather than trying to prevent Arrow from adding them.

This is essentially always an environment problem on the self-hosted agent, not something wrong in your repo. "not a .ql/.qls file, a directory, or a query pack specification" means the CodeQL CLI couldn't resolve `python-security-extended.qls` to anything usable - typically because the CodeQL bundle/CLI version on your self-hosted agent doesn't match what the Advanced Security Analyze task expects, so the built-in query pack isn't where that version looks for it, or the pack itself never fully downloaded (self-hosted runners need outbound network access to fetch CodeQL query packs, not just to clone your repo - check firewall/proxy rules on the EC2 box). Fix: update the CodeQL bundle on the agent to match the Advanced Security extension, clear any cached CodeQL query pack directory and let it redownload, and confirm the agent can reach the CodeQL pack registry over HTTPS. If a hosted Microsoft-managed agent run works fine, that confirms it's this agent's setup, not your configuration.

data.ilearner is Azure ML Studio/Designer's own internal serialization format for its built-in modules (like Boosted Decision Tree Regression) - a proprietary format, not a LightGBM model file, even though the underlying algorithm is gradient-boosted trees. That's why lgb.Booster(model_file="data.ilearner") fails with "Unknown model format": LightGBM's loader only understands its own text/binary format, not Azure's. There is no supported converter from .ilearner to .pkl - Microsoft hasn't published that internal format for third-party use. Practical paths: (1) in the Designer pipeline, add a "Convert Model to ONNX" step if your module supports it, then load with onnxruntime instead of joblib; (2) skip the built-in Designer training module entirely and train the equivalent model yourself in an Execute-Python-Script or Azure ML notebook step using scikit-learn's GradientBoostingRegressor or LightGBM directly, then call joblib.dump() yourself - that guarantees a real, portable model.pkl instead of relying on a conversion path that doesn't exist.

The general approach is sound and matches what dedicated tools (e.g. Spek, 'Lossless Audio Checker') already do: transcoded/fake-high-bitrate audio usually shows a hard, abrupt frequency cutoff well below the theoretical Nyquist limit, because lossy encoders discard everything above some cutoff (~16kHz around 128kbps MP3, ~19kHz around 192-256kbps), and re-encoding to a higher bitrate/lossless container afterward can't restore that missing content. Suggestions: work directly on the FFT of the PCM you already decode in read_audio_chunk rather than parsing the rendered spectrogram PNG - faster and more precise than image analysis. Sample multiple chunks across the track, since quiet intros/outros or sparse passages can mimic a cutoff. The main edge case: genuinely quiet, bass-heavy, acoustic, or classical material can legitimately have little high-frequency energy even when truly lossless, so key on a sharp cutoff/knee shape rather than low overall high-frequency energy. Treat results as a heuristic flag for manual review, not proof of transcoding.

You need transpose(1,2,0) before reshaping, not just reshape or a plain .T:
arr.transpose(1, 2, 0).reshape(8, 3)
arr has shape (3,4,2) - axis 0 is the letter (a/b/c), axes 1-2 are the (4,2) grid. transpose(1,2,0) moves the letter axis to the end, giving shape (4,2,3) where the last axis is now [a,b,c] for each position, while the first two axes still iterate in the original a1,a2,...,a8 order. Reshaping that to (8,3) flattens the (4,2) part into 8 rows while keeping each row's 3 letter-values together, giving exactly ['a1','b1','c1'], ['a2','b2','c2'], ..., ['a8','b8','c8']. Plain .reshape() or .ravel().reshape() (what you tried) doesn't work because reshape only changes how existing memory is grouped without reordering elements - you must physically permute axes with transpose first so the values you want adjacent in the output are actually adjacent in traversal order.

Plain Python import machinery isn't actually confused here - `importlib.import_module("Mod1").Module` and `..."Mod2").Module` really are two distinct classes/objects; sys.modules caches by the string you pass, so there's no accidental sharing at that level. The 'cross-talk' is almost certainly Kivy's own doing: Factory and the kv language resolve widget classes by class name in one single global registry/rule table, not per-module - so if both files define `class Module(...)` and either has a matching `<Module>:` kv rule (via Builder.load_string/load_file), the second one loaded silently overwrites or gets matched against the first's kv styling, regardless of which Python module object you hold a reference to. That's why renaming the classes (your commented-out Module1/Module2 workaround) fixes it: it removes the name collision in Kivy's global namespace. Keep class names (and any associated kv rule names) unique across dynamically loaded plugin modules; don't rely on a fixed literal class name as your plugin convention.
